Why Body Systems Matter in Sport

Every movement you make in sport — a sprint finish, a tackle, a shot at goal — depends on at least four body systems working in harmony. Sport scientists, physiotherapists and coaches all need a solid understanding of how these systems are structured before they can make sense of how the body responds to exercise. This lesson focuses on the body system structures you are required to know: the skeletal system, the muscular system, the cardiovascular system and the respiratory system.

The Skeletal System

The skeleton is the body's rigid framework. It is made up of 206 bones in an adult and is divided into two main parts: the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribcage) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs, shoulder girdle, pelvis). Bones are classified by their shape. Long bones — such as the femur, humerus, tibia and fibula — act as levers during movement. Short bones (wrist and ankle bones) absorb shock. Flat bones — the cranium, scapula, ribs and pelvis — protect vital organs. Irregular bones include the vertebrae of the vertebral column. The main bones you must know are: the cranium (skull), clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, ribs, vertebral column, pelvis, femur, patella (kneecap), tibia and fibula.

Key Fact

The main bones you must know are: cranium, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, ribs, vertebral column, pelvis, femur, patella, tibia and fibula. Work from head to toe and you will not miss any.

Types of Joint and Synovial Joint Structure

Where two or more bones meet, a synovial joint allows free movement. All synovial joints share the same basic structure: a joint capsule encloses the joint, lined by the synovial membrane which secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish the articular cartilage. Articular (hyaline) cartilage covers the ends of bones, reducing friction. Ligaments connect bone to bone, stabilising the joint. The three synovial joint types you need to know are: ball and socket joints (shoulder and hip — allow movement in all planes), hinge joints (knee and elbow — allow flexion and extension only) and pivot joints (top of the vertebral column/atlas and axis — allow rotation).

A synovial joint contains six key structures that work together to allow smooth, pain-free movement. The joint capsule is a tough fibrous sleeve enclosing the whole joint. Inside it, the synovial membrane produces synovial fluid — a viscous liquid that lubricates and delivers nutrients to the articular cartilage. Articular cartilage (hyaline cartilage) coats the bone surfaces, reducing friction and absorbing compressive forces during impact. Ligaments are strong bands of connective tissue that hold bone to bone, preventing dislocation. Some joints also contain bursae (fluid-filled sacs) to cushion areas of friction, and in the knee, fibrocartilage menisci deepen the joint surface and distribute load.

The Muscular System

There are three types of muscle tissue in the body. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and contracts involuntarily and continuously throughout life. Smooth muscle lines internal organs such as blood vessels and the digestive tract and also works involuntarily. Skeletal (voluntary) muscle is attached to bones via tendons and is under conscious control — it is the type of muscle used in all voluntary sporting movements.

The major voluntary muscles you must locate are: biceps (front of upper arm — flexes the elbow), triceps (rear of upper arm — extends the elbow), deltoids (top of the shoulder — abducts the arm), pectorals/pectoralis major (chest — adducts and rotates the arm), abdominals (abdomen — flex the trunk and stabilise the core), quadriceps (front of the thigh — extends the knee), hamstrings (rear of the thigh — flexes the knee), gastrocnemius (calf — plantarflexes the ankle), gluteals/gluteus maximus (buttocks — extends and externally rotates the hip), and latissimus dorsi (broad muscle of the back — pulls the arm downward and backward). The spec also includes trapezius (upper back and neck — elevates and retracts the scapula).

Key Fact

The major muscle groups are: biceps, triceps, deltoids, pectorals, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi and trapezius. For each one, know its location on the body.

Muscle Fibre Types

Skeletal muscle fibres are not all identical. The specification distinguishes two main types. Type I (slow-twitch) fibres contract slowly, generate less force but are very resistant to fatigue. They are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, giving them a red appearance, and they rely predominantly on aerobic respiration. They are well suited to endurance activities such as marathon running or cycling. Type II (fast-twitch) fibres contract rapidly and generate greater force but fatigue quickly. They rely more on anaerobic respiration and are recruited during high-intensity, short-duration activities such as sprinting or weightlifting.

The Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system consists of the heart, blood vessels and blood. The heart is a four-chambered pump located in the chest cavity, slightly left of centre. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the vena cava. From there it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, then passes through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle — the most powerful chamber — which pumps blood around the entire body through the aorta. The left ventricle has much thicker walls than the right because it must generate higher pressure for systemic circulation.

Blood travels through three types of vessel. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; their thick, elastic walls absorb the surge of pressure from each heartbeat. Veins carry blood back towards the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls and contain valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are microscopic, single-cell-thick vessels that form networks within tissues, allowing the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nutrients between the blood and cells. Blood itself is composed of red blood cells (carry oxygen via haemoglobin), white blood cells (immune defence), platelets (clotting) and plasma (the liquid carrying nutrients and waste).

Arteries have three distinct wall layers: a tough outer adventitia, a thick middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic tissue (tunica media), and a smooth inner endothelium. This construction allows them to expand and recoil with each heartbeat (the pulse you feel at your wrist is an artery). Veins share the same three layers but their tunica media is much thinner — they operate at low pressure and rely on skeletal muscle contractions and one-way valves to return blood to the heart. Capillaries are just one cell thick (endothelium only), with no muscle or connective tissue layers. Their tiny diameter (7–10 micrometres) means red blood cells pass through in single file, maximising contact time with surrounding cells for efficient gas and nutrient exchange.

The Respiratory System

The respiratory system draws oxygen into the body and expels carbon dioxide. Air enters through the nose and mouth and passes down the larynx (voice box) into the trachea (windpipe), a rigid tube kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. At the base of the trachea the airway divides into the left and right bronchi (singular: bronchus), each leading into its respective lung. Inside each lung the bronchi branch repeatedly into progressively narrower bronchioles, ending in tiny air sacs called alveoli.

The alveoli are the functional units of gas exchange: their enormous combined surface area (approximately 70 m² in an adult), moist thin walls and rich capillary network allow oxygen to diffuse from air into blood and carbon dioxide to diffuse from blood into air. The two lungs sit within the ribcage; the right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two (to accommodate the heart). Breathing itself is driven by the diaphragm — a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle beneath the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, it increases thoracic volume, drawing air in (inspiration). When it relaxes and rises back, thoracic volume decreases, forcing air out (expiration). The intercostal muscles between the ribs assist this process by lifting and lowering the ribcage.

Why Functions Matter

Understanding how each body system works is the foundation of sport science. Coaches, physiotherapists and athletes all need to know what each system does — not just what it is made of — so they can explain why performance improves with training, or why it breaks down with fatigue. This lesson examines the four key systems: skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory, and explores the specific jobs each one carries out during sport and exercise.

Functions of the Skeletal System

The skeletal system performs six important functions. First, it provides support — the vertebral column and leg bones act as a structural framework that holds the body upright against gravity, which is essential for every sporting activity from swimming to weightlifting. Second, it offers protection to vital organs: the cranium shields the brain, the ribcage guards the heart and lungs, and the vertebral column protects the spinal cord. Third, bones create movement through levers — they act as rigid levers that muscles pull on to generate movement at synovial joints. Every time a sprinter drives their leg backward or a tennis player swings their racket, a lever system is at work.

Fourth, the skeleton provides the body with its structural shape — the characteristic human silhouette is determined by bone structure, and this shape influences posture and aerodynamic efficiency in sport. Fifth, certain bones — particularly the long bones such as the femur and humerus, and flat bones such as the sternum — contain red bone marrow that carries out blood cell production. Red blood cells manufactured here carry oxygen to working muscles, making this function directly relevant to aerobic performance. Sixth, bones act as a mineral store, holding approximately 99% of the body's calcium and significant amounts of phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when needed and are also essential for normal muscle contraction.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeletal system are: support, protection, movement through levers, structural shape, blood-cell production in red bone marrow, and mineral storage (especially calcium and phosphorus). All six may be tested in short-answer questions.

Functions of the Muscular System

The muscular system's primary function is to produce movement through contraction. Muscles can only pull — they cannot push — so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs. At the elbow, the biceps acts as the agonist during flexion, shortening to bend the arm, while the triceps acts as the antagonist and relaxes to allow the movement. During extension — for example, a basketball chest pass — the roles reverse. The specification requires knowledge of antagonistic action at both the elbow and the knee (quadriceps and hamstrings). Muscles also have synergist muscles that assist the agonist, and fixator muscles that stabilise the joint to allow efficient movement.

Beyond movement, the muscular system maintains posture — deep postural muscles such as the abdominals, erector spinae and trapezius are in a state of continuous partial contraction to hold the body in alignment during both rest and activity. Good posture reduces injury risk and improves mechanical efficiency in sport. The muscular system also plays a major role in generating heat. Muscle contractions are only about 25% mechanically efficient — the remaining 75% of the energy released is lost as heat. This thermogenic function helps the body maintain its core temperature during exercise in cold environments, which is why vigorous activity warms you up rapidly.

Key Fact

Muscular system functions: movement via contraction (agonist/antagonist pairs), maintaining posture through continuous partial contraction, and generating heat as a by-product of muscle metabolism. At the knee, quadriceps = agonist for extension; hamstrings = agonist for flexion.

Functions of the Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system (the systemic or pulmonary circulatory system) has three core functions. Its primary role is the transport of oxygen and nutrients to working muscles and organs. During exercise, cardiac output increases — the heart beats faster and pumps more blood per beat (stroke volume) — so that oxygen and glucose reach the muscles rapidly enough to sustain contraction. Without this delivery, muscles would switch to anaerobic metabolism and fatigue rapidly.

The second function is the removal of waste products, including carbon dioxide and lactic acid produced during exercise. Deoxygenated blood carrying CO2 returns via the veins to the right side of the heart, from where it is pumped to the lungs (the pulmonary circuit) to release CO2 and collect fresh oxygen. Lactic acid is transported to the liver for conversion. The third function is regulation of body temperature. When the body overheats during exercise, vasodilation occurs — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, bringing warm blood to the surface where heat can be lost to the environment. When the body is cold, vasoconstriction narrows these vessels to retain core heat. This temperature-regulation mechanism is directly assessable in the written examination.

Vasodilation is the widening of blood vessels — particularly those supplying the skin — which allows more warm blood to reach the surface so that heat can radiate away from the body into the environment. This is why the skin looks flushed and red during or after vigorous exercise. Vasoconstriction is the opposite: blood vessels narrow, restricting blood flow to the skin and extremities so that warm blood is redirected to the vital organs and working muscles, conserving core temperature in cold conditions or at rest. Both processes are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and happen automatically in response to changes in core and ambient temperature. Understanding this mechanism is essential for explaining why a long-distance runner may feel warm even in cold weather.

Functions of the Respiratory System

The respiratory system drives breathing — the mechanical process of moving air in and out of the lungs. During inspiration (breathing in), the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract to lift the ribcage outward and upward, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity. This reduces internal air pressure below atmospheric pressure, so air rushes into the lungs. During expiration (breathing out), the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, the ribcage drops inward and downward, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is forced out. At rest this happens around 12-20 times per minute; during intense exercise breathing rate can exceed 40-50 breaths per minute.

The second and most critical function is gaseous exchange at the alveoli. The alveoli are surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the high concentration inside the alveoli across the thin alveolar wall into the blood (where oxygen concentration is lower), binding to haemoglobin in red blood cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide — in high concentration in the blood after being produced by working muscles — diffuses in the opposite direction, from the blood into the alveoli, and is then expelled during expiration. This process of diffusion is passive and depends on the concentration gradient being maintained: the continuous flow of blood removes oxygenated blood and brings fresh deoxygenated blood, keeping the gradient steep and exchange efficient.

The cardiovascular and respiratory systems are inseparable partners — together they form the cardiorespiratory system. The respiratory system gets oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide at the alveoli; the cardiovascular system then transports that oxygenated blood to the muscles and returns deoxygenated blood back to the lungs. During exercise, both systems respond simultaneously: breathing rate and depth increase to bring more oxygen to the alveoli, while heart rate and stroke volume increase to deliver more oxygenated blood to the working muscles. If either system fails to keep up — for example, if breathing rate cannot rise quickly enough — performance drops and the athlete enters anaerobic metabolism more quickly. Exam questions often require you to link both systems when explaining why performance changes with exercise intensity.

Why Does Your Body Change During Exercise?

The moment you begin exercising, your body's systems react almost instantly to match the increased demand for energy and oxygen. These immediate responses — which reverse quickly once you stop — are called the short-term effects of exercise. Understanding them is essential for any coach or athlete who wants to explain why warm-ups, pacing and hydration matter so much in practice. The key systems affected are the cardiovascular system, the cardio-respiratory system, and the muscular-skeletal system.

Cardiovascular Changes

Your heart is a pump, and during exercise it needs to deliver far more oxygen-rich blood to your working muscles. It achieves this in three linked ways. First, your heart rate increases — the number of beats per minute rises from a typical resting rate of around 60-80 bpm to well over 150 bpm during intense activity. Second, stroke volume — the amount of blood pushed out per beat — also increases because adrenaline and returning venous blood cause the heart to contract more forcefully. Third, these two changes multiply to produce a much higher cardiac output, calculated as heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. A trained athlete can increase cardiac output from roughly 5 litres per minute at rest to over 20 litres per minute during maximal exercise.

Another important cardiovascular short-term effect is the redistribution of blood flow. At rest, blood is shared fairly evenly across all the organs. During exercise, blood vessels supplying the working muscles vasodilate (widen), while vessels to less active organs such as the digestive system vasoconstrict (narrow). This redirection ensures that the muscles receiving the hardest workload get the greatest share of oxygen and nutrients at the time they are needed most.

Key Fact

Cardiac output = Heart rate × Stroke volume. During intense exercise, both heart rate and stroke volume increase, so cardiac output rises dramatically. Blood is simultaneously redirected (vasodilation) towards working muscles and away from non-essential organs (vasoconstriction).

Cardio-Respiratory Changes

Your muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide during exercise. The cardio-respiratory system responds by increasing both the rate and depth of breathing. Breathing frequency (breaths per minute) rises sharply — from around 12-20 breaths per minute at rest to 40-60 during hard exercise. At the same time, tidal volume — the amount of air moved in a single breath — increases because the diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract more powerfully. Together, a higher breathing rate and a greater tidal volume produce a large increase in minute ventilation (the total volume of air breathed per minute), ensuring that oxygen supply and carbon dioxide removal keep pace with the energy demands of the working muscles.

Increased body temperature is an inevitable by-product of the chemical reactions that release energy during exercise. The cardiovascular system helps manage this through vasodilation of blood vessels near the skin, allowing more heat to radiate away. Sweating is the other key cooling mechanism: sweat glands release water onto the skin surface, which evaporates and carries heat away from the body. This is why staying hydrated during exercise is so important — losing too much fluid through sweat reduces blood volume, which in turn makes it harder for the heart to maintain cardiac output.

Key Fact

Minute ventilation increases during exercise because breathing rate AND tidal volume both rise. Body temperature also increases, triggering vasodilation near the skin and sweating — the body's main mechanisms for temperature regulation during exercise.

Muscular-Skeletal Changes and Muscle Fatigue

As exercise intensity rises, the working muscles receive an increased supply of oxygen and nutrients thanks to vasodilation and the higher cardiac output described above. The muscles also become warmer, which temporarily increases their elasticity — they can stretch and contract more efficiently, reducing injury risk. However, if exercise is intense or prolonged, the muscles eventually begin to fatigue. Muscle fatigue is the inability to maintain the required force output, and athletes experience it as a burning sensation, a feeling of heaviness, and a progressive loss of power and coordination.

At high exercise intensities, when the cardio-respiratory system cannot deliver oxygen quickly enough to match demand, the muscles switch to anaerobic respiration. One waste product of this process is lactic acid. As lactic acid accumulates in the muscle tissue and bloodstream, it reduces the ability of the muscle fibres to contract effectively, contributing to the burning sensation and fatigue. The point at which lactic acid accumulates faster than the body can remove it is sometimes called the lactate threshold — going beyond this threshold rapidly accelerates fatigue. Lactic acid is eventually cleared during recovery through increased breathing and blood flow, which is one reason a gentle cool-down is important after intense exercise.

Once exercise intensity drops, the body enters a recovery phase in which oxygen consumption remains elevated — known informally as excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC). During this period, increased breathing rate and blood flow deliver extra oxygen to the muscles, which is used to convert the accumulated lactic acid back into glycogen (stored energy) in the liver. This process is why heart rate and breathing rate stay elevated for several minutes after exercise has stopped, and why a light cool-down jog is more effective than stopping abruptly — it keeps blood flowing and speeds lactic acid removal.

At low intensities (e.g. a brisk walk), heart rate and breathing rate rise modestly, energy is supplied almost entirely aerobically, and lactic acid stays below the lactate threshold. At moderate intensities (e.g. a steady run), heart rate and tidal volume are noticeably elevated, sweating begins, and muscles start to warm up significantly. At high intensities (e.g. a 400m sprint), cardiac output is near its maximum, breathing rate and tidal volume are at peak, lactic acid accumulates rapidly, and muscle fatigue sets in quickly. The exam may ask you to compare the responses at different intensities — always link the cardiovascular, respiratory and muscular systems together in your answer for higher marks.

Why Does the Body Change With Training?

When you exercise repeatedly over weeks and months, your body does more than just cope — it permanently rebuilds itself to handle the demands you place on it. These permanent structural and functional changes are called long-term adaptations. They are the physiological reason why a trained athlete performs far better than an untrained person of the same age and size. Understanding these adaptations helps coaches design effective training programmes and helps athletes appreciate why consistency is essential.

Cardiovascular Adaptations

The heart is a muscle, and like any muscle it responds to repeated overload by growing stronger. Cardiac hypertrophy is the thickening and enlargement of the heart muscle, especially the walls of the left ventricle. A hypertrophied heart pumps a greater volume of blood with each beat, so it needs to beat fewer times per minute to circulate the same amount of blood. This is why trained endurance athletes often have a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute — a condition known as bradycardia. For an elite cyclist or marathon runner, resting heart rates of 40–50 bpm are normal.

Linked to cardiac hypertrophy is an increase in stroke volume — the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle in a single beat. Because the ventricle has enlarged and its walls are stronger, it can fill with more blood and expel it more forcefully. Increased stroke volume means the heart achieves the same cardiac output at a lower heart rate, reducing the strain on the myocardium. Recovery after intense exercise also improves: a trained heart returns to its resting rate more rapidly because its larger stroke volume clears excess oxygen debt more efficiently. Faster recovery is therefore a direct consequence of cardiac hypertrophy and increased stroke volume working together.

Key Fact

Cardiac hypertrophy (a stronger, larger heart) leads to increased stroke volume, which in turn produces a lower resting heart rate (bradycardia) and faster recovery after exercise. These four cardiovascular adaptations are directly connected.

Respiratory Adaptations

Regular aerobic training strengthens the respiratory muscles — including the diaphragm and intercostal muscles — and increases lung capacity. Vital capacity, the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation, increases with training. Trained athletes can move more air per breath, meaning they can deliver more oxygen to the alveoli with each respiratory cycle. The alveoli also adapt: the number and density of capillaries surrounding the alveolar walls increases through a process called capillarisation. With more capillaries in close contact with the alveoli, gas exchange — the diffusion of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out — becomes faster and more efficient. The result is that a trained athlete extracts a greater proportion of oxygen from each breath.

Increased lung capacity and capillarisation work together during intense exercise: when oxygen demand spikes, the trained respiratory system can meet it more readily, delaying the onset of fatigue and allowing higher training intensities to be sustained. This improved respiratory efficiency is particularly important in endurance sports such as long-distance running, cycling and swimming, where prolonged aerobic effort places the greatest strain on the oxygen-delivery system.

Key Fact

Increased vital capacity and capillarisation of the alveoli are the two main respiratory long-term adaptations. They work together to increase the rate and efficiency of gas exchange, delivering more oxygen to the bloodstream per breath.

Musculoskeletal Adaptations

Resistance training causes muscle hypertrophy — an increase in the cross-sectional area of individual muscle fibres, particularly type II (fast-twitch) fibres. Hypertrophied muscles generate greater force, giving the athlete increased muscular strength. Endurance training increases muscular endurance by improving the muscles' mitochondrial density and glycogen storage capacity, allowing them to sustain repeated contractions for longer without fatiguing. Alongside muscle hypertrophy, capillarisation occurs within the muscles themselves: new capillary networks grow between muscle fibres, improving oxygen and nutrient delivery and accelerating the removal of carbon dioxide and waste metabolites. This muscular capillarisation is distinct from alveolar capillarisation but equally important for sustaining performance.

The skeleton and connective tissue also adapt. Repeated mechanical loading during weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) to lay down extra mineral, resulting in increased bone density. Denser bones are stronger, more resistant to fracture, and less susceptible to stress injuries. The tendons and ligaments that support the joints also become thicker and stronger through regular training, providing better joint stability and reducing the risk of sprains and ruptures. These connective tissue adaptations are slower to develop than cardiovascular changes but are vital for long-term athletic durability.

During high-intensity anaerobic exercise, glucose is broken down without sufficient oxygen, producing lactic acid as a by-product. Lactic acid dissociates into lactate and hydrogen ions; it is the accumulation of hydrogen ions that lowers muscle pH and causes the burning sensation associated with fatigue. Regular high-intensity training triggers several adaptations that raise the point at which lactic acid begins to accumulate (the lactate threshold). Trained muscles have more mitochondria, allowing a greater proportion of energy to be produced aerobically even at higher exercise intensities, so less lactic acid is generated. The muscles also become more efficient at buffering (neutralising) hydrogen ions and at clearing lactate by converting it back to glucose in the liver. The practical result is that a trained athlete can sustain a higher workload before feeling the effects of lactic acid accumulation, directly improving performance in repeated-sprint sports and endurance events alike.

The dominant adaptations depend on the training method used. Endurance athletes (e.g. long-distance runners, cyclists) experience the greatest improvements in cardiac hypertrophy, stroke volume, bradycardia, vital capacity, alveolar capillarisation and lactic acid tolerance — all of which support sustained aerobic effort. Resistance athletes (e.g. weightlifters, rugby forwards) experience pronounced muscle hypertrophy, increased bone density and stronger tendons and ligaments, as the primary demand is generating force rather than sustaining prolonged cardiovascular output. Team-sport athletes (e.g. footballers, basketball players) gain a broad range of adaptations because their training combines aerobic conditioning with repeated high-intensity sprints and contact work. A well-designed training programme matches the training method to the desired adaptation, following the principle of specificity.

What Is Health and Fitness?

Before looking at individual components, it helps to understand what we mean by the two terms. Health is a broad concept — it refers to complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not just the absence of illness. Fitness, by contrast, is the ability to meet the demands of a specific sport or task. A person can be healthy without being particularly fit, and a very fit athlete can still have health concerns. In sport, coaches and sport scientists care about both — but fitness components are what they measure and train.

Health-Related vs Skill-Related Components

The components of fitness are divided into two groups. Health-related components underpin general physical wellbeing and are relevant to everyone, whether or not they play sport: aerobic endurance (cardiovascular endurance), muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and body composition. Skill-related components are performance-oriented — they are most important for sport and physical activity: speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, and reaction time. In the written exam you may need to classify a component into the correct group, so knowing both lists is essential.

Key Fact

Health-related components (5): aerobic endurance, muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, body composition. Skill-related components (6): speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, reaction time.

Health-Related Components in Detail

Aerobic Endurance (Cardiovascular Endurance)

Aerobic endurance is the ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a prolonged period of exercise. It is sometimes called cardiovascular endurance. It is essential for activities that last a long time at a moderate-to-high intensity — marathon running, long-distance cycling and rowing all demand high aerobic endurance. A footballer also needs aerobic endurance to maintain their performance level across a full 90-minute match.

Muscular Endurance

Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to perform repeated contractions over a sustained period without becoming fatigued. It differs from muscular strength, which is about maximum force in a single effort. Sports that require muscular endurance include distance swimming, road cycling and cross-country running, where the same muscles must contract hundreds or thousands of times. A rower performing a 2,000-metre race needs high muscular endurance in the back, core and arm muscles to maintain stroke power throughout.

Muscular Strength

Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert in a single contraction. It is important in sports that involve lifting, throwing, sprinting or explosive contact. A shot-putter needs very high muscular strength to generate force through the put. A weightlifter, a rugby forward clearing out a ruck or a gymnast holding a static position all depend heavily on muscular strength.

Flexibility

Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint. It is determined by the elasticity of the muscles, tendons and ligaments surrounding the joint. High flexibility reduces injury risk and can improve performance in sports where large ranges of movement are needed. Gymnastics and dance demand exceptional flexibility — a gymnast performing a full split or a diver entering a pike position both require high flexibility. Even team sport players benefit from good flexibility to avoid muscle strains and to move efficiently.

Body Composition

Body composition refers to the ratio of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone, organs and fluid) in the body. It is a health-related component because a high proportion of body fat is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease and reduced health, while a favourable body composition supports physical performance. Optimal body composition differs by sport — a heavyweight powerlifter may have a higher body mass with large muscle mass, while a distance runner is typically lean with a low body fat percentage to reduce the mass that must be carried over distance.

Skill-Related Components in Detail

Speed

Speed is the ability to move the whole body, or a body part, from one point to another in the shortest possible time. A sprinter needs exceptional whole-body speed over 100 metres. A cricket or baseball batter needs high arm speed to swing the bat effectively, while a defender in football must have speed to track runs from attackers. Speed is most obviously tested by sprint tests such as a 30-metre sprint.

Power

Power is a combination of strength and speed — it is the ability to apply maximum force at speed in a single explosive movement. A high jumper needs power in their take-off leg to propel them upwards; a tennis player needs power in their shoulder and arm to drive a serve; a sprinter's start reaction out of the blocks is powered by a powerful leg drive. Power is measured by the vertical jump test or the standing broad jump.

Agility

Agility is the ability to change body position or direction quickly and precisely while maintaining control and balance. It combines speed, coordination and balance, making it one of the most sport-specific attributes tested. A basketball player dribbling past defenders, a netball player evading a marker or a rugby player stepping around a tackle all demonstrate high agility. The Illinois agility test is the standard assessment used to measure it.

Key Fact

Agility is the ability to change direction quickly and with control — it is a skill-related component because it depends on coordination and balance as well as speed. It is most important in sports that involve frequent changes of direction, such as basketball, netball and rugby.

Balance

Balance is the ability to maintain the centre of mass over the base of support, either while stationary (static balance) or while moving (dynamic balance). A gymnast holding a handstand or a figure skater landing a jump must have excellent static and dynamic balance. A surfer maintaining their position on a board demonstrates dynamic balance. Balance is commonly assessed using the stork stand test, which measures the ability to balance on one leg for as long as possible.

Coordination

Coordination is the ability to use two or more body parts smoothly and efficiently at the same time in a controlled movement. Hand-eye coordination is crucial in racket sports, cricket batting and goalkeeping, where the hands must track and respond to a moving ball. Foot-eye coordination is essential for football and rugby. Coordination is measured by the alternate hand throw test, in which the performer throws and catches a ball alternately with each hand.

Reaction Time

Reaction time is the time taken from the moment a stimulus is detected (such as a starting gun, an opponent's movement or a ball being released) to the start of the response. A sprinter must react instantly to the starting pistol; a goalkeeper must react to a shot from close range; a badminton player must react to a fast smash. Faster reaction time can make the difference between reaching a ball or missing it. It is assessed using the ruler drop test.

Most team sports require a blend of several components. In football, aerobic endurance (90-minute match demands), speed (chasing the ball or outrunning defenders), agility (changing direction in tight spaces), coordination (controlling the ball) and reaction time (responding to a through ball) are all highly relevant. Muscular strength and power matter for heading, shooting and winning physical battles. The balance of components differs by position — a goalkeeper prioritises reaction time and power; a central midfielder prioritises aerobic endurance; a striker prioritises speed and agility. In the exam you may be asked to select and justify the most important component for a given position or sport, so always link your choice back to the demands of the role.

The demands of a sport determine which fitness components are most critical. A 100-metre sprinter needs maximal speed and power but relies far less on aerobic endurance because the race lasts under 11 seconds — the ATP-PC and anaerobic energy systems dominate. A distance swimmer needs high aerobic endurance and muscular endurance but does not need exceptional agility or reaction time. A gymnast requires elite flexibility, balance and coordination but is less dependent on cardiovascular endurance. Understanding this link between sport demands and fitness requirements is central to planning effective training programmes — a coach would waste time training a shot-putter for aerobic endurance when their event demands strength and power.

Why Do We Test Fitness?

Fitness testing is used to measure the components of health and fitness in a structured, repeatable way. Before a coach or sport scientist can design a training programme, they need objective data — numbers that show exactly where an athlete's strengths and weaknesses lie. Testing also provides a baseline measurement that future test scores can be compared against. Crucially, fitness tests only give meaningful information when they are both valid and reliable. A test that varies due to warm-up differences, time of day or examiner technique cannot be fairly compared to previous results or to normative data tables.

Aerobic Endurance Tests

Two tests measure cardiovascular endurance. The multistage fitness test (also called the bleep test or 20-metre shuttle run) requires the participant to run between two lines 20 metres apart, keeping pace with an audio recording that plays beeps at increasing intervals. The speed increases each minute (each level) and the test ends when the participant can no longer reach the line in time or voluntarily drops out. The level and shuttle number at which the participant stops is recorded and compared to normative data tables to give a rating from very poor to excellent. The test is progressive and maximal, making it highly specific to aerobic endurance.

The Cooper 12-minute run offers an alternative. The participant runs as far as possible in exactly 12 minutes on a measured track. The total distance covered (in metres) is recorded and matched against normative data by age and gender. A well-conditioned male aged 15–16 might cover over 2,800 metres; a score below 2,100 metres would be rated poor. The test is simple to administer and requires only a stopwatch and a measured surface.

Key Fact

Two tests measure aerobic (cardiovascular) endurance: the multistage fitness test (20-metre shuttle run with progressive beeps, record the level/shuttle reached) and the Cooper 12-minute run (record total distance covered). Both use normative data tables to rate the result.

Flexibility, Muscular Endurance and Strength Tests

The sit-and-reach test measures flexibility of the lower back and hamstrings. The participant sits on the floor with legs straight and feet flat against a sit-and-reach box. They reach forward with both hands as far as possible along the measuring scale and hold the position for two seconds. The furthest point reached (in centimetres) is recorded — positive values are beyond the feet, negative values fall short. Three attempts are usually made and the best score used. Results are compared to normative data tables by age and gender.

Muscular endurance is measured with either the one-minute press-up test or the one-minute sit-up test. For press-ups, the participant begins in the standard press-up position (or box position for females in some versions) and performs as many full-range press-ups as possible in 60 seconds — chest to the floor and arms fully extended on each repetition. For sit-ups, the participant lies on their back with knees bent at 90 degrees and hands placed on thighs; they curl up until the hands reach the knees, then lower back down. The number of complete repetitions in 60 seconds is recorded and compared to normative data.

Muscular strength is tested either using a grip dynamometer or a one-repetition maximum (one-rep max). In the grip dynamometer test, the participant holds the device at their side and squeezes as hard as possible for a few seconds; three attempts are taken (alternating hands) and the best score (in kilograms) is recorded. The one-rep max test requires the participant to lift the heaviest single repetition possible for a given exercise (e.g. bench press or squat); this is found by working up in weight until only one full repetition can be completed with correct technique. Results are compared to normative data relative to the participant's body weight.

Speed, Power, Agility, Balance and Reaction Time Tests

The 30-metre sprint test measures speed. The participant starts from a standing position and sprints flat-out over 30 metres; time is recorded using either manual stopwatches or electronic timing gates. Three trials are usually taken and the best time used. Results are compared to normative data tables by age and gender — an elite youth sprinter might record under 4.0 seconds.

Power (explosive strength) is most commonly assessed using the vertical jump test (also called the Sargent jump). The participant stands next to a wall, reaches as high as possible with one hand and marks the reach height (chalk or measuring tape). They then jump as high as possible from a standing position and mark the peak jump height. The difference between the two heights (in centimetres) gives the jump height, which is recorded and compared to normative data. The standing broad jump is an alternative power test where the participant jumps horizontally from a standing position and the distance from the take-off line to the nearest landing point is measured.

The Illinois agility run measures agility — the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while moving at speed. The participant lies face down at the start line. On the signal, they sprint to the far end of the course, weave around a series of cones placed in a set pattern, and sprint back to the finish. The time taken (in seconds) is recorded. A typical course is 10 metres long and 5 metres wide; the total run with the cone weave covers approximately 60 metres of movement. Results are compared to normative data by age and gender.

Balance is measured using the stork stand test. The participant stands on their dominant foot with the other foot resting flat against the inside of the supporting knee, hands placed on the hips. On the signal they raise their heel and balance on the ball of the foot; the timer starts when the heel lifts and stops when balance is lost (heel touches ground, non-supporting foot moves, or hands leave hips). Three attempts are made and the best time (in seconds) is recorded and compared to normative data.

Key Fact

Speed = 30-metre sprint (record best time). Power = vertical/Sargent jump (difference between standing reach and jump height). Agility = Illinois agility run (weave cones, record time; start lying down). Balance = stork stand (balance on ball of dominant foot, record time). Reaction time = ruler drop test (record distance converted to milliseconds).

Reaction time is tested with the ruler drop test. The tester holds a ruler vertically at the 0 cm mark between the participant's open thumb and forefinger at the 0 cm level without touching it. Without warning, the tester drops the ruler and the participant catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler fell (in centimetres) is recorded; this is converted to reaction time in milliseconds using a standard conversion table (for example, a drop of 15 cm corresponds to approximately 175 milliseconds). Five trials are taken and the average used. The test is simple but has limited reliability if the tester gives visual cues before releasing.

Normative Data and Why It Matters

Normative data allows a raw test result to be given context. A grip strength reading of 40 kg means little on its own, but compared to a normative table it might be rated as above average for a 16-year-old male. Normative data also allows coaches to set realistic goals and to monitor progress over time. However, comparisons are only valid when testing conditions are standardised — the same warm-up, equipment, time of day and examiner technique must be used each time. Any change in conditions threatens the reliability and therefore the validity of the comparison.

A test is valid if it actually measures the component it claims to measure. For example, the sit-and-reach test is a valid measure of lower-back and hamstring flexibility — but it is not a valid measure of shoulder flexibility. A test is reliable if repeated testing under the same conditions produces the same result. Reliability can be threatened by factors such as varying warm-up duration, different equipment calibration, inconsistent instructions from the tester, or the participant's physical state on the day. If a test is reliable but not valid, it is measuring the wrong thing consistently. If it is valid but not reliable, results will fluctuate for reasons unrelated to actual fitness changes. Both properties are required before test data can be meaningfully compared with normative tables or previous personal scores.

The one-rep max test is arguably the hardest to standardise safely because the participant must work to their absolute maximum, increasing injury risk, and "full range of motion" can be interpreted differently by different testers. The ruler drop test is susceptible to anticipation — if the tester gives a visual cue (e.g. a slight finger movement before releasing), the participant may react to the cue rather than the drop, giving a falsely fast score. The stork stand can be affected by the surface — a soft mat versus a hard floor changes the difficulty significantly. In an exam, showing awareness that each test has potential threats to reliability will earn higher marks on evaluate questions.

Why Do We Test Fitness?

Fitness testing is a core tool in any serious training programme. Rather than guessing whether a performer is getting fitter, a coach can use objective data to make decisions that are evidence-based and precise. When used properly, test results drive every stage of the coaching cycle — from identifying what needs work, to setting goals, to measuring whether training is actually producing results. Understanding why fitness testing matters, and how to use results wisely, is essential knowledge for anyone working in sport and coaching.

Establishing a Baseline

Before any training programme begins, a coach must know where the performer currently stands. This starting-point measurement is called a baseline. Without a baseline, it is impossible to measure progress — a performer might feel fitter after six weeks of training, but only test scores recorded at the start can prove it. The baseline also allows the coach to identify which components of fitness are already at an acceptable level and which urgently need development. For example, a netball player might score well on agility but poorly on cardiovascular endurance; the baseline reveals this immediately.

Once a baseline is recorded, the same tests are repeated at regular intervals throughout the programme. This is called monitoring progress. Comparing repeated test scores against the baseline tells the coach and performer whether training is producing the desired adaptations. If scores stagnate or decline, it signals that the programme needs adjusting — perhaps by increasing intensity, changing training methods or addressing recovery.

Key Fact

The six reasons for fitness testing are: to carry out comparisons against normative data, to identify a performer's strengths and weaknesses, to provide a baseline for future comparisons, to provide important information for the coach, to provide information that assists in team selection, and to set goals or targets.

Identifying Strengths and Weaknesses

Fitness testing allows a coach to build a detailed profile of a performer across all relevant components. For instance, a footballer might be tested on speed (30m sprint), agility (Illinois agility run), cardiovascular endurance (multistage fitness test), and muscular strength (hand grip or rep max). The results show which components are a strength and which are a weakness that limits performance. This targeting prevents training from becoming unfocused. A coach will not waste a sprinter's limited training time on flexibility work if speed is the weakness that most affects their event. Testing turns vague impressions into specific, actionable priorities.

Setting Goals with SMART Targets

Without test data, goal-setting tends to be vague — "get fitter" or "run faster" give a performer no clear direction. Test results make it possible to set SMART targets: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-phased. For example, if a basketball player scores 9 shuttles on the multistage fitness test, a SMART short-term target might be "reach level 10 within eight weeks." This is specific (multistage test level 10), measurable (an objective number), achievable and realistic (one level above current), and time-phased (eight weeks). SMART goals give the performer something concrete to aim at, which research consistently links to better exercise adherence and effort in training.

Test results also help a coach design and adapt the training programme itself. If a swimmer's repeat sprint data shows that their lactate threshold is lower than expected, the coach can introduce more aerobic interval work at the appropriate training zone. As fitness improves, re-testing allows the programme to be updated — loads, rest periods or methods can be adjusted to match the performer's current level, ensuring continued progression rather than a plateau.

Key Fact

SMART targets turn raw test scores into meaningful goals. A baseline test result is the starting point; the SMART target describes the desired test result by a specific future date. The coach then designs the training programme to close the gap between the two.

Motivating the Performer

Seeing measurable improvement is one of the most powerful motivators in sport. When a performer's re-test results show that their sit-up score has increased from 32 to 45 in six weeks, the data provides concrete evidence that their hard work is paying off. This boosts confidence and sustains engagement with the programme. Conversely, when results plateau, the data can motivate a performer to refocus and try harder. Many coaches share test results openly with their athletes precisely for this motivational effect, using progress charts to make improvements visible.

Team Selection and Normative Data

Fitness test results provide information that assists with team selection. A coach selecting players for a squad can use objective data to compare performers against each other rather than relying on subjective impressions from matches. Test scores can also be compared against normative data — published tables of average scores for a test, broken down by age and gender. Normative data shows whether a performer's result is poor, average, above average or excellent compared with the wider population or with elite performers in their sport. For example, a 16-year-old male who scores a vertical jump of 50 cm can compare this against published normative tables to see that this sits in the "above average" category.

Validity and Reliability of Testing

Validity refers to whether a test genuinely measures what it is supposed to measure. A test is valid if the component it measures directly reflects what is required in the performer's sport. For example, the multistage fitness test has high validity for sports that require sustained cardiovascular endurance, such as distance running or football. However, it would have low validity if used to assess muscular strength — it simply does not measure that component.

Reliability refers to the consistency of a test — if the same performer takes the same test under the same conditions on two occasions, a reliable test will produce very similar scores. Reliability is affected by factors such as the time of day the test is taken, the performer's hydration and fatigue levels, the equipment used, and whether the tester follows a standardised protocol. If a test is not reliable, then comparing results across time or between performers becomes meaningless. A coach who discovers their testing procedure is inconsistent cannot trust the data, and any conclusions drawn — about progress, goal-setting or selection — will be flawed.

Normative data is only useful if the test that produced your result was administered in exactly the same way as the test that produced the normative data. If a performer completes the sit-and-reach flexibility test on a cold day without warming up, but the normative table was built from scores taken after a 10-minute warm-up, the comparison is invalid. This is why standardising test protocols — same time of day, same warm-up, same equipment, same instructions — is essential. Validity matters here too: a poorly chosen test that does not reflect the relevant component will produce a score that cannot be meaningfully placed against normative data for that component. Coaches must always use a recognised, standardised protocol to ensure both validity and reliability before trusting any comparison.

A coach typically uses a battery of tests — several different tests covering multiple components — at the start of a training block to build a full fitness profile. The results are recorded, compared against normative data, and used to set SMART targets for each component. As the programme progresses, the same tests are repeated (often every four to six weeks) and the results are compared to the baseline. The coach can then make informed decisions: increase load if progress is slower than expected, introduce new training methods if one component is not responding, or ease volume if recovery data suggests fatigue is accumulating. This cycle of test, analyse, adapt and re-test is the backbone of evidence-based coaching.

Why Planning Ahead Matters

Before a coach writes a single session plan, they must gather information about the performer they are working with. Jumping straight into training without this groundwork is ineffective at best and dangerous at worst. A training programme that ignores a performer's medical history, current fitness level, lifestyle or available resources will fail to produce results — and may even cause harm. The factors to consider fall into two broad groups: personal factors (relating to the individual) and environmental factors (relating to the setting and resources available).

Health Screening and the PAR-Q

The first step in any new training programme is a PAR-Q (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire). This is a short questionnaire that asks about symptoms such as chest pain, dizziness, bone or joint problems, and whether a doctor has ever advised against vigorous exercise. A 'yes' answer to any question does not automatically prevent someone from training, but it flags that medical clearance should be sought before they begin. The PAR-Q protects both the performer and the coach: if a participant suffers an adverse event during training and no health screening was completed, the coach may face professional or legal consequences. Health screening more broadly includes checking for medical conditions such as asthma, diabetes or a known heart condition, each of which will influence the type, intensity and duration of training that is appropriate.

Key Fact

The PAR-Q is completed before starting any new training programme. It screens for medical conditions and cardiovascular risk factors. A 'yes' answer means the performer should seek medical advice before training begins.

Current Fitness Level and Test Results

Once health screening is complete, the coach needs to establish a baseline — a starting point from which progress can be measured. This means carrying out appropriate fitness tests (such as the multi-stage fitness test for cardiovascular endurance or the sit-and-reach for flexibility) and recording the results. Knowing the performer's current fitness level allows the coach to set training at an appropriate intensity — too easy and no adaptation will occur; too hard and the performer risks injury or drop-out. Test results also highlight specific strengths and weaknesses, so the programme can target the components of fitness most relevant to the performer's sport.

Goals and SMART Targets

Understanding what the performer wants to achieve is essential before any programme is written. Goals should be set using the SMART framework: Specific (clearly defined, e.g. 'improve 10 km run time'), Measurable (tracked with a number or test result), Agreed/Achievable (agreed between coach and performer, and within reach), Realistic (attainable given the performer's current level and resources) and Time-phased (with a clear deadline). SMART targets improve exercise adherence — performers who have a clear goal are more motivated and more likely to stick to the programme. Setting both short-term targets (e.g. improve press-up score by 10 in six weeks) and a longer-term goal (e.g. complete a 10 km race in under 50 minutes by the end of term) helps maintain focus and momentum throughout training.

Personal Factors: Age, Gender, Lifestyle and Time Available

Beyond health and goals, the coach must consider a range of personal factors. Age affects the type of training that is safe and effective: younger athletes with developing bodies may need to avoid heavy resistance work, while older performers have reduced muscle elasticity and need more recovery time between sessions. Gender influences physiological differences in average strength, hormonal profile and some injury susceptibilities, and should inform exercise selection and intensity guidance. Lifestyle — covering factors such as diet, sleep patterns, work or school commitments, stress levels and social habits — determines how much the performer can recover between sessions. A performer who sleeps poorly, eats erratically and has a physically demanding job will need a lighter training load than someone with a healthy routine and plenty of rest. Time available for training and the cost of training are practical limits: the programme must be realistic about how many sessions per week a performer can commit to, and what resources they can afford.

Key Fact

Personal factors include health, fitness, age, gender, lifestyle, time available for training and cost of training. Each one can limit or shape what a training programme looks like in practice.

Environmental Factors: Facilities, Equipment and the Sport's Demands

Even a perfectly designed programme is useless if the performer cannot access the facilities or equipment needed to carry it out. Environmental factors include the availability of a swimming pool, gym, track, sports hall or open space, and the equipment (resistance machines, free weights, agility ladders, etc.) that the performer can use. The coach must also analyse the demands of the sport: a swimmer needs cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance training, whereas a sprinter needs power, speed and explosive strength work. Designing a programme without analysing what the sport actually requires means training the wrong components.

Safety, Injury Risk and Warm-Up/Cool-Down

Safety must be considered at every stage of programme design. Before training begins, the coach should carry out a risk assessment — checking facilities, equipment, participant numbers and the environment for hazards. A performer with a known vulnerability (a previous knee injury, for example) needs a programme that avoids aggravating that area. Warm-up and cool-down must be built into every session: a warm-up raises heart rate and temperature, increases blood flow to muscles and reduces injury risk, while a cool-down gradually lowers heart rate, removes metabolic waste products from working muscles and aids recovery. Skipping these components significantly increases both acute and overuse injury risk.

A risk assessment before a training session involves four key checks: facilities (are surfaces safe, is space adequate, is the venue free from trip hazards?), equipment (is it in good repair, correctly adjusted and appropriate for the participants?), participants (are there any medical conditions, previous injuries or fitness concerns that change what is safe for this group?) and rules or laws (does the activity comply with health and safety regulations and the sport's governing body guidelines?). A written risk assessment protects participants and demonstrates the coach's duty of care. Even for informal training sessions, mentally running through these checks before starting is good professional practice.

A training programme that a performer cannot sustain financially or logistically will fail, regardless of its scientific soundness. If a coach prescribes five gym sessions per week but the performer can only afford two visits and has school commitments every evening, adherence will collapse. Cost of training covers gym membership fees, equipment purchases, travel, specialist coaching and competition entry fees. Time available must account for school or work, family responsibilities, travel to training venues and recovery time. The best coaches design programmes that fit the performer's real life — not an idealised schedule. A realistic but consistent programme will always outperform a perfect programme that is abandoned after two weeks.

Why Principles Matter

Any training programme can make an athlete fitter — for a while. But without a structured framework, progress stalls, performance peaks prematurely, or the athlete risks injury through poorly judged workloads. The principles of training give coaches a shared language and a set of rules to design programmes that produce genuine, lasting gains. Each principle addresses a different risk: specificity guards against wasted effort, overload drives adaptation, reversibility reminds us that fitness is temporary, variance keeps athletes engaged, and individual needs ensure the programme fits the person, not just the sport.

Specificity

Specificity states that the body adapts specifically to the type of stress placed upon it. A long-distance runner who only does weight training will develop muscular strength but will not improve cardiovascular endurance — they have trained the wrong system. A coach applying specificity asks: What energy systems does this sport primarily use? What muscle groups are most important? What movement patterns must be replicated? A basketball coach, for example, would design drills involving explosive lateral movements, short sprints and jumping — not long, steady-state running — because those match the physiological and technical demands of the game. Specificity also applies to position: a goalkeeper's training programme will differ markedly from a midfielder's even within the same sport.

Progressive Overload

The body adapts to a given training load and then reaches a plateau. To keep improving, the load must be progressively increased — this is progressive overload. Overload means working at a level above what the body is accustomed to; progressive means the increase is gradual and planned rather than sudden. A swimmer who completes 20 lengths per session without discomfort must eventually swim 22, then 24 lengths to continue improving. If the overload is too rapid, the risk of injury rises sharply; if it is absent, fitness stagnates. Progressive overload is the engine of fitness improvement and is closely linked to the FITT principle, which gives coaches four specific handles to control the overload applied.

Key Fact

The FITT principle provides four variables a coach can manipulate to apply progressive overload: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), and Type (which training method). Increasing any one of these variables increases the training load on the athlete's body.

The FITT Principle

The FITT principle gives a coach four specific levers to increase training load in a controlled way. Frequency is how often an athlete trains — moving from three sessions a week to four increases the total weekly training stimulus. Intensity is how hard the athlete works — a runner increasing their average pace from 8 km/h to 9 km/h imposes a greater cardiovascular demand. Time refers to the duration of each session — extending a session from 30 minutes to 45 minutes adds volume. Type is the training method selected — switching from continuous running to interval training recruits the anaerobic energy system more heavily and creates a different physiological adaptation. Coaches rarely change all four variables simultaneously; instead, they adjust one or two each week or training block to ensure overload is applied safely and systematically.

Reversibility

Fitness is not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced, the body reverses its adaptations — cardiovascular endurance declines, muscle mass decreases and flexibility is lost. This is the principle of reversibility, sometimes described with the phrase "use it or lose it". Research suggests cardiovascular fitness begins to decline noticeably within two to three weeks of inactivity, while strength losses are slightly slower but still significant within four to six weeks. A coach managing a swimmer recovering from illness must plan a structured return to training, gradually rebuilding the load rather than expecting the athlete to resume immediately at their previous level. Reversibility also underlines the importance of rest and recovery being planned — complete rest for weeks at a time is rarely beneficial.

Key Fact

Reversibility means that fitness gains built through months of training can be lost within weeks if training stops. Cardiovascular endurance declines fastest — noticeable changes occur within two to three weeks — while strength takes slightly longer to reverse.

Variance (Tedium)

Repeating exactly the same sessions week after week causes two problems: physical plateauing, as the body adapts completely to a familiar stimulus, and psychological tedium, as athletes lose motivation through repetition. The principle of variance — sometimes called the principle of tedium — requires coaches to introduce variety into training to prevent both. A football coach might rotate between circuit training, fartlek running, small-sided games and plyometric sessions during a pre-season block. Varying the type of training also ensures that multiple components of fitness are developed — not just the one or two that appear in the regular session format. Importantly, variance should not mean randomness; sessions should still follow specificity and progressive overload principles — variety is introduced within a structured plan.

Individual Needs

No two athletes are identical. Their current fitness levels, injury history, age, gender, role in the sport, goals and available training time all differ. The principle of individual needs states that a training programme must be tailored to the specific performer, not applied generically. A 16-year-old beginner taking up rugby will require a very different programme from a 22-year-old experienced player preparing for a county trial — even if both play the same position. A coach who ignores individual needs risks under-challenging a fit athlete (who will plateau and become bored) or over-loading a less-fit one (who risks injury and burnout). Fitness testing data — gathered from tests such as the multistage fitness test or the Illinois agility run — gives a coach the objective baseline they need to set genuinely individual training loads.

Rest, Recovery and Applying the Principles

Progressive overload works only if adequate rest is built into the programme. During exercise, muscle fibres are stressed and micro-damaged; it is during recovery that the body repairs and strengthens these fibres, producing the adaptation that improves fitness. Without sufficient rest, the cumulative damage exceeds the body's repair capacity, leading to overtraining, fatigue and injury. A coach designing a weekly programme for a 100-metre sprinter might schedule three high-intensity sessions with rest or light activity days between them, allowing full neuromuscular recovery before the next intense stimulus. Rest is not wasted training time — it is when the adaptations triggered by overload actually take place. A well-designed programme applies all five principles together: it is specific to the sport, progressively overloaded via FITT, varied to maintain motivation, and tailored to the individual — with rest built in at every stage.

Imagine a coach preparing a recreational cyclist for a 10-week sportive ride. In week one, the athlete trains three times a week (frequency), at a moderate steady pace (intensity), for 40 minutes per session (time), using continuous cycling (type). By week six the coach has increased frequency to four sessions, pushed intensity into threshold pace for intervals, extended two sessions to 60 minutes, and introduced interval training to target the aerobic-anaerobic boundary. Each change is deliberate — only one or two FITT variables change in any given training block, so the coach can identify what is driving improvement and avoid over-loading the athlete. This systematic adjustment is exactly what the exam expects candidates to be able to describe and apply to a given scenario.

When training load is increased too sharply — more than roughly 10% per week as a general guideline — the cumulative stress on muscles, tendons and bones exceeds the body's ability to repair itself. The result is overtraining syndrome: persistent fatigue, declining performance, irritability, suppressed immune function and a significantly elevated injury risk. Common overtraining injuries include stress fractures, tendinopathy and muscle strains. This is why progressive overload must be gradual and why rest days are non-negotiable components of any well-designed programme. A good coach monitors signs of overtraining (flat performance, low mood, disturbed sleep) and is prepared to reduce load — temporarily applying the principle of reversibility deliberately to allow full recovery.

Why Do Different Athletes Train Differently?

Not every athlete trains the same way — a marathon runner, a sprinter and a gymnast all have very different physical demands. Each training method targets a specific component of fitness and is therefore suited to particular sports and performers. Knowing which method to use — and why — is a key skill for coaches and performers alike. This lesson covers the main methods of training and their advantages.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a constant, moderate intensity for a prolonged period — usually 20 minutes or more — without rest intervals. It is the most commonly associated method with cardiovascular endurance because it keeps the heart rate elevated steadily within the aerobic training zone. The advantages of continuous training include its simplicity (no specialist equipment needed), low cost, and the fact it can be done almost anywhere. It is particularly popular with distance runners, cyclists and swimmers. A marathon runner such as Eliud Kipchoge would use long, steady runs to develop their aerobic base and cardiovascular endurance.

Fartlek Training

The word "fartlek" comes from Swedish and means "speed play". Fartlek training combines steady-paced aerobic running with unplanned or planned bursts of faster effort, such as sprinting to a lamp post or accelerating uphill. It develops both cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance, making it ideal for games players who have to switch between different intensities. Advantages include variety (which reduces boredom), flexibility (the performer chooses when to sprint) and its ability to replicate the unpredictable demands of team sports. A football midfielder or rugby player benefits greatly from fartlek sessions because match play involves constant changes of pace.

Key Fact

Continuous training stays at a constant moderate pace; fartlek training mixes that steady pace with random bursts of higher intensity. Both methods develop cardiovascular endurance, but fartlek additionally improves speed endurance — making it more suitable for team-sport athletes.

Interval Training

Interval training involves alternating periods of high-intensity exercise with planned rest or low-intensity recovery periods. The work-to-rest ratio can be adjusted to target either the aerobic or anaerobic energy system depending on the intensity and duration of each interval. Shorter, more intense intervals (e.g. 30 seconds hard, 90 seconds rest) stress the anaerobic system, while longer intervals at a more moderate pace stress the aerobic system. The key advantage of interval training is its flexibility — coaches can precisely control the intensity, duration and number of repetitions to match the demands of the sport. A 400-metre runner might use 400 m repetitions with 3 minutes rest to develop their anaerobic threshold and speed endurance.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a specific form of interval training that uses very short bouts of near-maximal effort (typically 80–95% of maximum heart rate) separated by brief recovery periods. A common example is 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated 8 times (the Tabata protocol). HIIT primarily develops cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance simultaneously, and research shows it can achieve similar cardiovascular improvements to longer continuous sessions in a fraction of the time. Its main advantage is time efficiency. A footballer performing pre-season fitness work might use HIIT sprints to rapidly improve both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power.

Key Fact

HIIT is a specific, high-intensity variant of interval training. The key difference is that HIIT demands near-maximal effort during every work phase, making sessions much shorter but equally (or more) effective than longer aerobic workouts. Both HIIT and interval training can be adapted to improve aerobic or anaerobic components depending on the work-to-rest ratio used.

Circuit Training

Circuit training uses a series of exercise stations performed one after another, with minimal rest between stations. Each station targets a different muscle group or fitness component, so the body is kept working throughout. Circuits typically develop muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance at the same time, and can be adapted to include power or strength exercises. The advantages of circuit training include variety, the ability to train a large group simultaneously, and its adaptability — stations can be changed to suit any sport. A netball or basketball team might use circuit training in pre-season to build both aerobic fitness and muscular endurance across the whole body.

Weight / Resistance Training

Weight (or resistance) training involves working muscles against an external load — such as free weights, machines or body weight — through a controlled range of movement. The primary component developed depends on the sets and repetitions used: heavy loads with few repetitions (e.g. 3 sets of 5) develop muscular strength, while moderate loads with higher repetitions (e.g. 3 sets of 15–20) develop muscular endurance. Resistance training also contributes to power when explosive movements such as Olympic lifts are incorporated. An advantage is that it is highly specific — coaches can target exactly the muscle groups used in a sport. A shot putter or a rugby prop would use heavy resistance training to build maximal muscular strength.

The relationship between load and repetitions determines whether resistance training builds strength, power or endurance. A heavy load lifted for very few repetitions (1–5 reps) maximises muscular strength gains by recruiting the highest-threshold motor units. A moderate load lifted for 8–12 repetitions is optimal for muscular hypertrophy (size). A lighter load lifted for 15–20 or more repetitions trains muscular endurance, as the muscles must sustain repeated contractions over time. Explosive movements performed with moderate loads — such as a power clean — train power. Coaches should match the load-rep scheme to the athlete's position and the demands of their sport.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training uses rapid stretching of a muscle followed immediately by an explosive contraction — a mechanism known as the stretch-shortening cycle. Examples include box jumps, bounding, depth jumps and clap press-ups. Plyometrics primarily develop power, which is the combination of strength and speed. They are particularly suited to athletes who need explosive movements — a high jumper, a basketball player or a volleyball player all require powerful jumps. An advantage is that plyometrics closely replicate the explosive demands of many sports, making them highly sport-specific. The main limitation is the high impact involved, so performers need a solid strength base before beginning plyometric training.

Flexibility Training

Flexibility training aims to improve the range of motion at joints. There are two main types specified. Static stretching involves holding a muscle in a lengthened position for typically 15–30 seconds; it is safe, easy to perform and effective at improving general flexibility. It is widely used in cool-downs and by gymnasts and dancers for whom a high range of movement is a core performance requirement. PNF stretching (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) is a more advanced technique that involves contracting the target muscle isometrically while it is stretched, then relaxing and deepening the stretch. PNF typically produces greater flexibility gains than static stretching and is often used by physiotherapists and elite athletes. A gymnast or a dancer would use both methods regularly to maintain and improve their flexibility.

PNF stretching exploits the nervous system to achieve a greater range of motion. The technique typically follows three phases: first, the muscle is passively stretched to its limit; second, the athlete isometrically contracts the stretched muscle for around 5–10 seconds (pushing against a partner's or immovable resistance), which temporarily fatigues the motor neurones; third, the muscle is relaxed and the partner deepens the stretch further, taking advantage of the brief window when the muscle's stretch reflex is suppressed. This "post-contraction inhibition" allows the muscle to lengthen further than a static stretch alone would achieve. PNF requires a trained partner and is more time-consuming, which is why it tends to be used in high-performance settings rather than in general warm-ups.
